en: The Sūtra on Impermanence Spoken by the Buddha, also known as the Sūtra of the Three Recitations,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree:
I bow my head and take refuge in the Unsurpassed One, Who constantly gives rise to the great compassionate mind of vast vows.
To rescue sentient beings from the stream of birth and death, And lead them to the secure and peaceful state of nirvāṇa;
With great equanimity to ward off wrongdoing, patience without weariness, The power of single-minded skillful means and right wisdom—
Since his self-benefit and benefit for others are both perfected, He is titled the Tamer and Teacher of Gods and Humans.
I bow my head and take refuge in the Treasury of the Sublime Dharma, Where the principles of three, four, two, and five are perfectly luminous;
Through seven and eight, one can open the gates of the Four Noble Truths, So that all who practice reach the shore of the unconditioned.
The Dharma-cloud and Dharma-rain moisten all living beings; They can eliminate feverish afflictions and dispel myriad ailments.
Those who are difficult to transform are made harmonious and compliant; Guiding according to their capacities, not by forceful means.
I bow my head and take refuge in the true Saṅgha, The eight classes of noble ones who have transcended defilement;
With the vajra-wisdom mallet they shatter the mountains of heterodoxy, Forever severing the entanglements of beginningless existence.

From the Deer Park to the Twin Trees, following the Buddha throughout his lifetime as he propagated the True Teaching, each has completed their transformative work according to their original conditions;
now their bodies are reduced to ashes and their wisdom extinguished, abiding in silent non-arising.
I prostrate with universal reverence to the Triple Gem, the Honored Ones; This is called the True Cause capable of universal salvation.
For those lost in the delusions of birth and death, forever submerged and drowning, May they all attain liberation and reach Bodhi.
All who are born must return to death; their countenances all undergo decay and decline.
When powerful strength is assailed by disease, none can escape this fate.
Even if Mount Sumeru, at the end of the kalpa, were to be utterly destroyed and scattered, [none could escape].
The great ocean, deep and bottomless, shall likewise be completely exhausted;
the great earth and the sun and moon, when their time comes, all return to extinction;
there has never been a single thing that has not been swallowed by impermanence.
From the highest realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception down to the Universal Monarch,
though the seven treasures always accompany them and a thousand sons constantly surround them,
when their lifespan is exhausted, it does not pause for even a moment.
They drift once more in the sea of death, Undergoing manifold sufferings according to conditions.
Circling within the three realms like a well-drawing wheel,
Or like a silkworm making its cocoon, Spinning silk that then binds itself.
Even the unsurpassed World-Honored Ones, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of Śrāvakas, must relinquish their impermanent bodies; how much more so for ordinary beings?
Parents and wives, brothers and kinsmen—[all are likewise impermanent].
Beholding with my own eyes the separation from birth and death, how could I not grieve and lament?
Therefore, I exhort all people: listen attentively to the true Dharma;
together abandon the realm of impermanence and proceed toward the gate of the deathless.
The Buddha-dharma is like nectar; it removes heat and brings cooling refreshment.
One should listen with single-minded devotion, for it can extinguish all afflictions.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three kinds of things in the world that are unlovely, lack luster, are not to be cherished, and are not to one's liking.”
What are these three?
They are old age, sickness, and death.
O bhikṣus, this old age, sickness, and death are truly unlovely in the world, truly lack luster, truly are not to be longed for, and truly are not to one's liking.

If old age, sickness, and death did not exist in the world, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would not appear in the world to teach sentient beings the Dharma he has realized and the matters of discipline.
Therefore, one should know that this aging, sickness, and death are unlovely, lack luster, are not to be cherished, and are disagreeable to all in the world.
By means of these three matters, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world to teach sentient beings the Dharma he has realized and the methods of discipline.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"External adornments all end in decay; The internal body’s transformation is likewise.
Only the Supreme Dharma does not perish; All wise people should examine this well."
This aging, illness, and death are universally loathed; their physical forms are so hideous as to be utterly repulsive.
The youthful countenance lasts but a moment, before all shall soon behold it withered and frail.
Even if one’s lifespan were to fill a hundred years, In the end, one cannot escape the pressure of impermanence;
The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death constantly follow, Perpetually bringing no benefit to sentient beings.

When the Blessed One had spoken this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and others, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Constantly seeking the objects of desire, one does not practice virtuous deeds;
how can one preserve the physical life when one does not see death approaching?
When the life-force and vital breath are about to end, all the limbs and joints shall be severed.
All sufferings accompany death; at this time, one can only sigh in regret.
Both eyes roll upward as the sword of death descends according to one's karma;
thoughts and intentions are filled with terror, and no one can provide rescue or relief.
Long gasps rattle the chest in haste; short breaths parch the throat.
The King of Death urges on his messengers, while kinsmen stand by in vain.
All consciousness grows dark and obscured as one enters the perilous city.
Relatives and friends all abandon him, leaving him to be dragged away by the ropes.
He is led before King Yama, where he receives retribution according to his karma:
through superior causes one is born in the good realms, while through evil karma one falls into hell.
No vision surpasses wisdom; no darkness exceeds ignorance;
no ailment exceeds the enemy; no terror exceeds death.
All who are born must surely die; those who commit evil suffer pain that cuts to the very core.
One should diligently exert oneself in the three types of action, constantly cultivating merit and wisdom.
When all kinsmen have departed and one's wealth is taken by others,
one should carry only one's own roots of goodness as provisions for the perilous path.
Just as a tree by the roadside provides a brief respite but not a long stay,
so too shall it be for chariots, horses, wives, and children before long.
Like a flock of birds that roost together at night and fly off in different directions at dawn, so it is with all things.
Death separates one from kin and friends; parting occurs in this same way.
Only the Buddha’s Bodhi is the true place of refuge and reliance.
I have briefly explained this according to the sūtras; let the wise reflect upon it well.
Devas, asuras, yakṣas, and others who have come to hear the Dharma, should listen with a sincere mind;
protect the Buddha-dharma so that it may endure long, and each of you diligently practice the teachings of the World-Honored One.
All you disciples who have come here, whether dwelling upon the earth or abiding in the air,
should always give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward the world of humans, and day and night abide yourselves in accordance with the Dharma.
May all worlds be ever peaceful and secure; May boundless merit and wisdom benefit all beings;
May all karmic offenses and afflictions be eliminated, And may they leave behind all suffering to return to perfect nirvana.
Constantly using the fragrance of precepts to polish and adorn the body, Always wearing the robes of meditative concentration to sustain the person,
Adorned everywhere with the wondrous flowers of Bodhi, One dwells in constant peace and happiness wherever one stays.
In the *Buddha-bhāṣita-anityatā-sūtra*, it is said: "If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, or an upāsaka or upāsikā, sees someone who is about to die and whose body and mind are afflicted by pain."
One should arouse a mind of loving-kindness to rescue, deliver, and benefit them.
Instruct them to bathe in fragrant water to become pure, put on fresh and clean garments, sit with composure, and contemplate with right mindfulness.
If the sick person lacks the strength to do so themselves, others should assist them in sitting.
If they are unable even to sit, simply have the patient lie on their right side, with palms joined and a sincere mind, facing the western direction.
Before the patient, select a pure location and smear the ground with fragrant cow-dung mud, making it as large or small as desired.
Form a mandala with square corners, scatter flowers upon the ground, burn various famous incenses, and light lamps at the four corners.

Within the mandala, suspend a painted image so that the patient may maintain a continuous stream of mental focus, perceiving its features with perfect clarity, and thereby inspire the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, he extensively explained that the three realms are difficult to dwell in and that the sufferings of the three miserable destinies are not places where one should be born; only the Buddha’s Bodhi is the true refuge.
Because of this taking of refuge, one will certainly be born in the buddha-fields of the ten directions, dwell together with bodhisattvas, and experience subtle and wondrous bliss.
He asked the sick person,
"In which Buddha-field would you now wish to be born?
The sick person replied:
"I wish to be born in such-and-such a Buddha-world.

At that time, the Dharma-preacher should, according to the patient's mental inclinations, proclaim for them the causes and conditions of the Buddha-lands, the sixteen contemplations, and so forth—explaining each detail as in the Western Land of Immeasurable Life—thereby causing the patient’s mind to rejoice in being born in that Buddha-land.
Having preached the Dharma for them, he further instructed them to contemplate with clarity the marks and signs of the Buddha’s body, regardless of which direction or country they were in.
Once they had contemplated these marks and signs, he further instructed them to request the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas, saying:
“I prostrate to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with all the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; may you take pity on me, deliver me, and bring me benefit.”
"I now respectfully invite you to extinguish all my transgressions;
furthermore, I shall take these disciples with me to be born in the Buddha-lands alongside the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He spoke thus a second and a third time.
Once the instruction has been given, he further directs the patient to recite the name of that Buddha.
When ten recitations are accomplished, he confers the Three Refuges and performs an extensive repentance.
Upon the completion of the repentance, he further administers the Bodhisattva precepts to the patient.
If a sick person is too distressed to speak, another may receive the precepts on their behalf and perform the repentance and so forth.
Provided that this is not done without sincere intent, the transgression will be extinguished and they shall obtain the Bodhisattva precepts.

Once the precepts have been received, support the sick person so that they lie with their head to the north and face toward the west. Whether the eyes are open or closed, they should clearly contemplate the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics of the Buddha; this should likewise be done for all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Furthermore, for their sake, he explains the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths, the twelve links of dependent origination from ignorance to old age and death, and contemplations on suffering, emptiness, and so forth.
If they are approaching the end of life, those attending the patient should simply recite the Buddha’s name, ensuring that the sound does not cease for even a moment.

However, when reciting the Buddha’s name, one should do so according to the patient's own inclination, reciting only that specific name and not those of other Buddhas, for fear that the patient’s mind might give rise to doubt and confusion.

As the life of that patient gradually draws to a close, they will immediately see transformed Buddhas and a multitude of Bodhisattvas, holding exquisite incense and flowers, coming to welcome the practitioner.

When the practitioner sees this, joy immediately arises; their body is free from pain and their mind is not distracted. With right view arising in the mind as if entering meditative absorption, they pass away shortly thereafter, and will certainly not fall back into the sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Riding upon the aforementioned teachings, one will be reborn before the Buddha in the time it takes a strong man to extend or contract his arm.

If there are lay *upāsakas* or *upāsikās*, after their death, one should take the deceased’s new and fine garments as well as personal belongings and divide them into three parts; for the sake of the deceased, these should be offered to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
By this means, the deceased’s karmic obstructions will be further exhausted, and they will obtain the benefits of superior merit and welfare.
One should not dress the corpse in fine garments or similar finery when conveying it away.
Why is this? Because it provides no benefit.

If a renunciant bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śrāmaṇera, or the like possesses clothing or non-clothing items, these shall be treated according to the various Vinaya teachings; in all other respects, they are the same as those of laypeople.

If one escorts the deceased to the place of enshrinement, they may be settled downwind, laid on their side in a lateral recumbent position with the right flank touching the ground and the face turned toward the sunlight.
On the upwind side, a high seat should be prepared and adorned in various ways.
Please request a bhikṣu capable of reciting scriptures to ascend the Dharma seat and recite the *Anityatā-sūtra* for the deceased.

The filial son should cease his grief and no longer weep; likewise, all others should with single-minded devotion burn incense and scatter flowers for the deceased, making offerings to the high seat, the sublime sūtras, and the bhikṣu. Thereafter, they should sit down, join their palms in reverence, and listen to the sūtra with a focused mind.
The bhikṣus should read it aloud slowly and thoroughly.

Upon hearing the sutra, each person should contemplate for themselves that their own body is impermanent and will soon be worn away and destroyed; mindful of detachment from the world, they should enter into samādhi.
Having finished reading this sutra, one should once again scatter flowers and burn incense as an offering.
Furthermore, one should request a bhikṣu to recite whichever mantra he knows twenty-one times over water that is free of insects, and then sprinkle it upon the deceased.
Furthermore, recite the mantra over clean yellow earth twenty-one times and scatter it over the body of the deceased.
Thereafter, act as you wish: either enshrine the remains within a stūpa, cremate them with fire, or place them in a śītavana (cemetery) or beneath the earth.

By the power of these causes and conditions of merit, may all the karmic obstacles of that deceased person—including the ten evil deeds, the four grave offenses, the five crimes of immediate retribution, and the slander of Mahāyāna sūtras—be extinguished all at once throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas.

In the presence of all Buddhas, they attain great merit, give rise to wisdom to sever delusions, and obtain the six supernormal powers as well as the knowledge of the three insights; they enter the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Traveling through the ten directions, they make offerings to all Buddhas, listen to and receive the true Dharma, and gradually cultivate and accumulate boundless merit and wisdom.
When you have finally realized unsurpassed bodhi, turned the wheel of the true Dharma to deliver immeasurable multitudes, and attained the most perfect enlightenment by entering great parinirvāṇa,
only then shall we part at the moment of death.
